pages.name: Your turn
pages.task: The same two machines, and 5 goes in. What drops out?
pages.why: `g` adds 4 to 5, so 9 sits on the join. `f` doubles that 9, so 18 drops out.

pages.text: Swap them and `f` doubles first, so 3 becomes 6 on the join and 10 drops out. Added first, the 4 was doubled to 8. Added last, it stays 4.

pages.name: Lesson 1's machine
pages.task: Lesson 1's machine, × 3 then − 1, turns 5 into 14. Swap the two boxes round. What drops out now?
pages.why: Swapped, `5 − 1 = 4` goes onto the join, and × 3 turns it into 12. In the first order `5 × 3 = 15` sat on the join and 14 came out.

pages.name: f of g of x
pages.text: Textbooks write this chain as `f(g(x))`, said ‘f of g of x’, and call it a [[composite function]]; UK books also write `fg(x)`. As with any bracket, the inside is worked first, so `g` goes first. Swapped, it is `g(f(x))`.
